title: Fault-tolerant quantum computation cannot be achieved with constant spacetime overhead
authors: Kishor Bharti, Tobias Haug, Andrew Tanggara
abstract: The threshold theorem states that quantum computations can be made reliable below a physical error threshold, at the cost of additional physical qubits and circuit depth. Recent work has reduced these space and time overheads to polylogarithmic or nearly logarithmic scalings, but whether the cumulative spacetime overhead can be constant has remained unclear. Here, we show that even for the simplest task of preserving quantum information in a quantum memory, under an optimistic noise model and allowing general adaptive protocols, there is an unavoidable logarithmic contribution to the cumulative spacetime overhead. This additional cost can nevertheless be shared among many logical qubits, so sufficiently wide computations, including standard implementations of Shor's algorithm, may still achieve constant relative overhead. We further give a positive-rate CSS code construction that attains the memory bound, identify sufficient conditions under which the same scaling extends from quantum memory to fault-tolerant circuit implementations, and derive circuit-size bounds for subsystem spacetime codes. Our work establishes fundamental limits on the resources required for quantum fault tolerance.
summary: This work establishes fundamental limits on the resources needed for fault-tolerant quantum computation, particularly concerning the overhead required for quantum memory. It proves that while constant *relative* overhead is possible for wide computations, an unavoidable logarithmic cost exists in the cumulative spacetime overhead. The findings provide crucial scaling laws for designing practical, large-scale quantum processors.
main_problem: The paper determines the fundamental limits on the cumulative spacetime overhead required for achieving fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_result: It shows that while constant *relative* overhead is achievable for sufficiently wide computations, an unavoidable logarithmic contribution to the cumulative spacetime overhead exists for quantum memory.
method: The analysis uses information-theoretic bounds derived from the probability of surviving erasure events and compares these to the required physical resources using adaptive protocol models and spacetime-code constructions.
model_or_system: The primary model is quantum memory—preserving an arbitrary quantum state for a duration $S$ under independent erasure noise. The analysis extends to general fault-tolerant circuits using spacetime-code descriptions.
key_observables: Minimum worst-case physical storage locations ($Cmin$), relative overhead ($ rac{Cmin}{KS}$), and physical circuit size ($	ext{CFT}$).
important_parameters: Logical qubit count ($K$), storage duration ($S$), target error ($\epsilon$), and the ratio $\log(S/\epsilon)/K$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes an optimistic noise model (independent erasure noise) and general adaptive protocols, though the limitation is argued to persist for general noise.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the optimal relative overhead controlled by the ratio $\log(S/\epsilon)/K$, showing a crossover point where constant relative overhead becomes possible.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the memory overhead bound ($	ext{Cmin}$), then extending this to general circuit overhead ($	ext{CFT}$), and finally analyzing the fundamental scaling using spacetime-code representations to derive the width-duration trade-off.
why_interesting: It establishes rigorous, fundamental resource bounds on the overhead required for fault tolerance, which directly impacts the feasibility estimates for large-scale quantum computation architectures.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The optimal relative overhead under independent erasure noise is controlled by the ratio log(S/ϵ)/K, where K is the number of logical qubits, S the storage duration and ϵ the target error. At the crossover K = Θ(log(S/ϵ)), the costs of retaining the logical information and maintaining reliability are comparable. For K = Ω(log(S/ϵ)), the relative overhead remains constant, whereas for K = o(log(S/ϵ)) the reliability cost dominates and the overhead grows logarithmically.
